    Ring Theory

    Introduction

    Ring theory studies various types of rings.

    The ring theory content in this article is inseparable from the divisibility theory in number theory. First, similar to normal subgroups in group theory, we first introduce the kernel of ring homomorphisms, which is called an ideal; in fact, this is the generalization of the concept of numbers in number theory to general rings. Then, to extend concepts like prime numbers, Euclidean algorithm, and prime factorization over the integer ring to general rings, we get concepts of different types of integral domains.

    Many conclusions in number theory still hold in other common rings. It can be said that one part of the work in ring theory is discussing whether these number theory conclusions can hold in general rings; if not, what restrictions need to be imposed on rings to make these conclusions hold.

    Notation

    When there is no ambiguity, this article may omit the multiplication symbol for rings, and will write the ring (𝑅, +, ⋅)(R,+,⋅) as the ring 𝑅R. In the ring 𝑅R, the additive identity is also called the zero element, denoted 00; the multiplicative identity is also called the unity element, denoted 11.

    The definition of rings in this article does not require a unity element

    Note that the definition of rings in this article does not require a unity element. Some articles require rings to contain a unity element, so the statements of some conclusions in this article need slight adjustment. For example, in this article, ideals can be defined based on subrings, but in other articles, they may need to be defined based on additive subgroups.

    Ideals

    Similar to the case of groups, we can establish the concepts of subrings and ring homomorphisms.

    Subring

    For a ring (𝑅, +, ⋅)(R,+,⋅) and its subset 𝑆S, if (𝑆, +, ⋅)(S,+,⋅) is also a ring, then 𝑆S is called a subring of 𝑅R.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z

    For any integer 𝑛n, 𝑛𝐙 ={𝑛𝑘 :𝑘 ∈𝐙}nZ={nk:k∈Z} is a subring of 𝐙Z.

    Ring Homomorphism

    For rings (𝑅, +, ⋅)(R,+,⋅) and (𝑆, ⊕, ⊙)(S,⊕,⊙), if 𝜋π preserves addition and multiplication, i.e., for all 𝑟1,𝑟2 ∈𝑅r1,r2∈R, 𝜋(𝑟1 +𝑟2) =𝜋(𝑟1) ⊕𝜋(𝑟2)π(r1+r2)=π(r1)⊕π(r2) and 𝜋(𝑟1 ⋅𝑟2) =𝜋(𝑟1) ⊙𝜋(𝑟2)π(r1⋅r2)=π(r1)⊙π(r2) both hold, then the map 𝜋 :𝑅 →𝑆π:R→S is called a homomorphism from ring 𝑅R to ring 𝑆S.

    When ring definitions require a unity element

    If ring definitions require a unity element, then the definition of ring homomorphisms often also requires that the unity element maps to the unity element. For homomorphisms between non-zero unital rings, this additional requirement only ensures that the homomorphism does not map the entire unital ring to zero.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z (continued)

    The map modulo any non-zero integer 𝑛n, i.e., 𝜋 :𝐙 →𝐙/𝑛𝐙π:Z→Z/nZ where 𝜋(𝑎) =¯𝑎π(a)=a¯, is a ring homomorphism.

    The discussion of the kernel and image of group homomorphisms can be almost entirely transferred here. The (relative) size of the image of a homomorphism determines whether the homomorphism is surjective, and whether the kernel is trivial determines whether the homomorphism is injective. The kernel of a ring homomorphism is defined as follows:

    Kernel of a Homomorphism

    For a homomorphism 𝜋 :𝑅 →𝑆π:R→S from ring 𝑅R to ring 𝑆S, the kernel is {𝑟 ∈𝑅 :𝜋(𝑟) =0}{r∈R:π(r)=0}, denoted ker⁡𝜋ker⁡π, where 00 is the additive identity of 𝑆S.

    Obviously, the kernel and image of a ring homomorphism are both subrings. Conversely, not all subrings can be the kernel of some ring homomorphism. Subrings that can be the kernel of a ring homomorphism are called ideals of the ring.

    Ideal

    For a ring 𝑅R and its subring 𝐼I, then 𝐼I is called

    • a left ideal if for all 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R, 𝑟𝐼 ⊆𝐼rI⊆I, where 𝑟𝐼 ={𝑟𝑎 :𝑎 ∈𝐼}rI={ra:a∈I};
    • a right ideal if for all 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R, 𝐼𝑟 ⊆𝐼Ir⊆I, where 𝐼𝑟 ={𝑎𝑟 :𝑎 ∈𝐼}Ir={ar:a∈I};
    • an ideal if 𝐼I is both a left ideal and a right ideal of 𝑅R.

    Here, we require that the ideal 𝐼I is closed under left multiplication and right multiplication by the ring 𝑅R. This condition is natural. Because elements in ideals map to zero under ring homomorphisms, and any number multiplied by zero on the left or right should equal zero, which is the required closure. Additionally, because the additive structure of rings is an abelian group, any subgroup is a normal subgroup; and the multiplicative structure of rings is very primitive and does not impose additional restrictions on substructures. This shows that the condition of being closed under left and right multiplication is also sufficient.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z (continued)

    As an example, the subring 𝑛𝐙nZ mentioned earlier is actually an ideal of 𝐙Z. It is the set of all multiples of 𝑛n. A multiple of 𝑛n, multiplied by any integer, yields a multiple of 𝑛n. In fact, all ideals of 𝐙Z are of this form, and such rings are called principal ideal domains. For general rings, some ideals are not the set of multiples of a single element; the existence of such general rings is precisely the original motivation for studying ideals (rather than simply studying multiples)4.

    Quotient Rings

    As with groups, based on ideals of rings, we can define the quotient ring on the set of all (additive group) cosets. Consider the set

    𝑅/𝐼={𝑎+𝐼:𝑎∈𝑅},R/I={a+I:a∈R},

    where the coset 𝑎 +𝐼 ={𝑎 +𝑏 :𝑏 ∈𝐼}a+I={a+b:b∈I}. It can be proven that the operations

    $$

    \begin{aligned} (a+I)+(b+I)&=(a+b)+I,\ (a+I)(b+I)&=(ab)+I \end{aligned} $$

    are well-defined, i.e., the results of these operations are independent of the choice of representatives in the cosets. Under these operations, 𝑅/𝐼R/I forms a ring. Again, consistent with the case of groups, we can establish the first isomorphism theorem for rings, and there exists a natural homomorphism from the ring to its quotient ring. These proofs show that ideals of rings and normal subgroups of groups play the same role in the homomorphisms of their respective structures.

    First Isomorphism Theorem

    Let 𝜋 :𝑅 →𝑆π:R→S be a homomorphism from ring 𝑅R to ring 𝑆S. Then ker⁡𝜋ker⁡π is an ideal of 𝑅R, and 𝑅/ker⁡𝜋 ≅𝜋(𝑅)R/ker⁡π≅π(R) is a subring of 𝑆S.

    Natural Homomorphism

    For a ring 𝑅R and its ideal 𝐼I, the map 𝜋 :𝑅 →𝑅/𝐼π:R→R/I given by 𝜋(𝑟) =𝑟 +𝐼π(r)=r+I is a surjective homomorphism from 𝑅R to 𝑅/𝐼R/I, called the natural homomorphism from 𝑅R to the quotient ring 𝑅/𝐼R/I.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z (continued)

    As an example, the ring of congruence classes modulo 𝑛n is 𝐙/𝑛𝐙Z/nZ, which is the quotient ring of 𝐙Z modulo its ideal 𝑛𝐙nZ. This also explains the meaning of the symbol 𝐙/𝑛𝐙Z/nZ. The modulo 𝑛n map 𝜋 :𝐙 →𝐙/𝑛𝐙π:Z→Z/nZ mentioned above is the natural homomorphism here, and the corresponding kernel is exactly the ideal 𝑛𝐙nZ.

    Other isomorphism theorems also hold for rings.

    Second Isomorphism Theorem

    Let ring 𝑅R have subring 𝐴A and ideal 𝐵B. Then 𝐴 +𝐵 ={𝑎 +𝑏 :𝑎 ∈𝐴,𝑏 ∈𝐵}A+B={a+b:a∈A,b∈B} is also a subring of 𝑅R, while 𝐴 ∩𝐵A∩B is an ideal of 𝐴A, 𝐵B is an ideal of 𝐴 +𝐵A+B, and (𝐴 +𝐵)/𝐵 ≅𝐴/(𝐴 ∩𝐵)(A+B)/B≅A/(A∩B).

    Third Isomorphism Theorem

    Let ring 𝑅R have ideals 𝐼,𝐽I,J with 𝐼 ⊆𝐽I⊆J. Then 𝐽/𝐼J/I is also an ideal of 𝑅/𝐼R/I, and (𝑅/𝐼)/(𝐽/𝐼) ≅𝑅/𝐽(R/I)/(J/I)≅R/J.

    Correspondence Theorem

    Let ring 𝑅R have ideal 𝐼I. Then there is a bijection between the set of all subrings S ={𝑆 :𝐼 ⊆𝑆 ⊆𝑅}S={S:I⊆S⊆R} of 𝑅R containing 𝐼I and the set of all subgroups T ={𝑇 :𝑇 ≤𝑅/𝐼}T={T:T≤R/I} of 𝑅/𝐼R/I. The bijection 𝜑 :S →Tφ:S→T maps 𝑆 ∈SS∈S to 𝑆/𝐼 ∈TS/I∈T. This bijection preserves inclusion relations, and ideals of 𝑅R always map to ideals of 𝑅/𝐼R/I.

    These theorems will play a fundamental role in discussing the structure of rings and ideals later.

    Operations on Ideals

    Various operations can be defined on ideals of rings. This is similar to how greatest common multiples and least common multiples can be defined on the divisibility structure of integers.

    Operations on Ideals

    Let 𝑅R have ideals 𝐼,𝐽I,J. The following operations can be defined:

    • The sum of ideals: 𝐼 +𝐽 ={𝑎 +𝑏 :𝑎 ∈𝐼,𝑏 ∈𝐽}I+J={a+b:a∈I,b∈J};
    • The product of ideals: 𝐼𝐽 ={∑𝑛𝑖=1𝑎𝑖𝑏𝑖 :𝑎𝑖 ∈𝐼,𝑏𝑖 ∈𝐽}IJ={∑i=1naibi:ai∈I,bi∈J}, i.e., the set of all finite sums of products of the form 𝑎𝑏ab;
    • The intersection of ideals: 𝐼 ∩𝐽I∩J.

    It is easy to verify that the results of these operations are still ideals of the ring.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z (continued)

    Consider the integer ring 𝐙Z. For ideals 𝑛𝐙nZ and 𝑚𝐙mZ, we have

    𝑛𝐙+𝑚𝐙=gcd(𝑚,𝑛)𝐙,(𝑛𝐙)(𝑚𝐙)=(𝑚𝑛)𝐙,(𝑛𝐙)∩(𝑚𝐙)=lcm(𝑚,𝑛)𝐙.nZ+mZ=gcd(m,n)Z,(nZ)(mZ)=(mn)Z,(nZ)∩(mZ)=lcm(m,n)Z.

    In general, for a ring 𝑅R and its ideals 𝐼I and 𝐽J,

    𝐼𝐽⊆𝐼∩𝐽⊆𝐼,𝐽⊆𝐼+𝐽.IJ⊆I∩J⊆I,J⊆I+J.

    Using these definitions, we can generalize the Chinese remainder theorem for integers to general rings. But before that, we need to further generalize concepts like prime numbers and coprimality to general rings.

    Maximal Ideals

    Through the structure of ideals of rings, we can understand the properties of rings.

    A non-zero ring 𝑅R always has two trivial ideals: {0}{0} and 𝑅R. If the ring 𝑅R is also commutative, then a ring with only these two ideals can only be a field1.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a commutative non-zero unital ring. Then 𝑅R is a field if and only if 𝑅R has only trivial ideals {0}{0} and 𝑅R.

    Proof

    If 𝑅R is a field, then for any non-zero ideal 𝐼I, we can take any non-zero element 𝑎 ∈𝐼a∈I. Then for any element 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R, we have 𝑟 =(𝑟𝑎−1)𝑎 ∈(𝑟𝑎−1)𝐼 ⊆𝐼r=(ra−1)a∈(ra−1)I⊆I, so 𝐼 =𝑅I=R. Conversely, for any 𝑎 ∈𝑅a∈R with 𝑎 ≠0a≠0, we can verify that 𝑎𝑅 ={𝑎𝑟 :𝑟 ∈𝑅}aR={ar:r∈R} is an ideal, which must equal 𝑅R. Therefore, there exists 𝑏 ∈𝑅b∈R such that 𝑎𝑏 =1ab=1, which shows that 𝑎a has an inverse, so 𝑅R is a field.

    The condition of commutative rings is necessary here; otherwise, we need to restrict both left ideals and right ideals to be trivial to ensure the ring is a division ring.

    This conclusion can be extended to cases where the ring itself is not a field. But at this time, we need to consider quotient rings, and discuss the condition for commutative non-zero unital quotient rings to be fields. The quotient ring 𝑅/𝐼R/I being a field means that 𝑅/𝐼R/I has only trivial ideals. According to the correspondence theorem, this means that there are no ideals in the original ring 𝑅R strictly between the ideal 𝐼I we mod out and 𝑅R itself. Such an ideal 𝐼I is called a maximal ideal.

    Maximal Ideal

    For a ring 𝑅R and its ideal 𝑀M, if 𝑀 ≠𝑅M≠R, and the only ideals of 𝑅R containing 𝑀M are 𝑀M and 𝑅R, then 𝑀M is called a maximal ideal.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a commutative non-zero unital ring with ideal 𝑀M. Then the quotient ring 𝑅/𝑀R/M is a field if and only if 𝑀M is a maximal ideal.

    Example: Integer Ring 𝐙Z (continued)

    For example, in the integer ring 𝐙Z, the ideal 𝑛𝐙nZ is a maximal ideal if and only if 𝑛n is a prime. For a prime 𝑝p, the quotient ring 𝐙/𝑝𝐙Z/pZ is a field, also denoted 𝐅𝑝Fp.

    Not all rings have maximal ideals, but non-zero unital rings always have maximal ideals.

    Theorem (Krull)

    For any ideal 𝐼 ≠𝑅I≠R of a non-zero unital ring 𝑅R, there always exists a maximal ideal 𝑀M of 𝑅R such that 𝐼 ⊆𝑀I⊆M holds.

    Proof

    The idea is to use Zorn's lemma. Consider the set SS of all proper ideals of 𝑅R (i.e., ideals not equal to 𝑅R) containing 𝐼I. Since 𝐼 ∈SI∈S, it is non-empty and forms a poset under inclusion. For any chain 𝐽0 ⊆𝐽1 ⊆⋯ ⊆𝐽𝑛 ⊆⋯J0⊆J1⊆⋯⊆Jn⊆⋯ in it, let their union be 𝐽J. It is easy to verify that this is also an ideal. Moreover, 𝐽 ≠𝑅J≠R, because otherwise 1 ∈𝐽1∈J, i.e., there exists 𝑛n such that 1 ∈𝐽𝑛1∈Jn, which contradicts 𝐽𝑛Jn being a proper ideal. Thus, by Zorn's lemma, there exists a maximal ideal 𝑀 ⊇𝐼M⊇I.

    Maximal ideals, analogous to irreducible elements in divisibility theory. This is because the inclusion relation of ideals is the divisibility relation of integers; no ideal as a superset is like a factor that cannot divide. However, the concept of maximal ideals is broader than that of irreducible elements because not all ideals are principal ideals.

    Prime Ideals

    The condition for fields is stricter than that for integral domains. Ideals that ensure the quotient ring is an integral domain are called prime ideals, which are analogous to the concept of prime numbers in divisibility theory.

    Prime Ideal

    For a commutative ring 𝑅R and its ideal 𝑃P, if 𝑃 ≠𝑅P≠R, and for any elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R, whenever 𝑎𝑏 ∈𝑃ab∈P holds, there is always 𝑎 ∈𝑃a∈P or 𝑏 ∈𝑃b∈P, then 𝑃P is called a prime ideal.

    This definition may seem somewhat abrupt, but comparing with the definition of prime numbers, this definition of prime ideals is also natural.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a commutative non-zero unital ring with ideal 𝑃P. Then the quotient ring 𝑅/𝑃R/P is an integral domain if and only if 𝑃P is a prime ideal.

    Proof

    For a commutative non-zero unital ring 𝑅R, the quotient ring 𝑅/𝑃R/P is an integral domain if and only if 𝑅/𝑃R/P has no zero divisors. Let the coset 𝑎 +𝑃a+P be denoted ¯𝑎a¯. The quotient ring 𝑅/𝑃R/P having no zero divisors is equivalent to ¯𝑎¯𝑏 =¯0a¯b¯=0¯ always implying ¯𝑎 =¯0a¯=0¯ or ¯𝑏 =¯0b¯=0¯. According to the correspondence theorem, this is equivalent to 𝑎𝑏 ∈𝑃ab∈P always implying 𝑎 ∈𝑃a∈P or 𝑏 ∈𝑃b∈P.

    In the integer ring 𝐙Z, 𝑛𝐙nZ is both a maximal ideal and a prime ideal if and only if 𝑛n is a prime. In general commutative rings, maximal ideals always imply prime ideals, but not conversely; this can be seen from the properties of their corresponding quotient rings.

    Theorem

    For a commutative non-zero unital ring 𝑅R, maximal ideals are necessarily prime ideals.

    Later, we will see that the converse only holds in rings with good properties sufficiently similar to the integer ring.

    Principal Ideals

    Similar to the concept of subgroups, in the discussion of rings, we often need to consider ideals generated by subsets.

    Ideal Generated by a Subset

    For a non-zero unital ring 𝑅R and its non-empty subset 𝐴 ⊆𝑅A⊆R, if 𝐼I is the smallest ideal of 𝑅R containing 𝐴A (with respect to inclusion), then 𝐼I is called the ideal generated by a subset 𝐴A, and denoted (𝐴)(A). At this time, 𝐴A is called the generating set of (𝐴)(A).

    Principal Ideal

    An ideal generated by a single element 𝑎 ∈𝑅a∈R is called a principal ideal, denoted (𝑎)(a). At this time, 𝑎a is called the generator of (𝑎)(a).

    For a set 𝐴A, we can describe its generated ideal. First, we have the following definitions

    $$

    \begin{aligned} RA&={r_1a_1+\cdots+r_na_n:r_i\in R,a_i\in A,n\in\mathbf Z},\ AR&={a_1r_1+\cdots+a_nr_n:r_i\in R,a_i\in A,n\in\mathbf Z}. \end{aligned} $$

    In fact, they are the left ideal and right ideal generated by 𝐴A respectively. Then, the ideal generated by 𝐴A is 𝑅𝐴𝑅RAR. For commutative rings, all these structures defined are the same.

    All ideals in the integer ring are principal ideals, often denoted as (𝑛)(n) below.

    Integral Domains

    An integral domain is a commutative, unital, non-zero ring without zero divisors. This concept is a generalization of the integer ring. However, the resulting ring may not be good enough to allow every conclusion from integer divisibility theory to be directly copied. To generalize number theory conclusions, we can further impose restrictions on integral domains. The three most common integral domains are Euclidean domains, principal ideal domains, and unique factorization domains; these concepts strictly contain each other.

    Divisibility Relations

    First, we generalize the relevant concepts from integer divisibility theory to general commutative rings.

    Divisibility

    Let a commutative ring 𝑅R have elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R. If there exists 𝑥 ∈𝑅x∈R satisfying 𝑎 =𝑏𝑥a=bx, then 𝑏b divides 𝑎a, denoted 𝑏 ∣𝑎b∣a. At this time, 𝑏b is called a divisor of 𝑎a.

    Associates

    Let a commutative ring 𝑅R have elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R. If they differ only by an invertible element, i.e., there exists an invertible element 𝑢 ∈𝑅u∈R satisfying 𝑎 =𝑏𝑢a=bu, then 𝑎a and 𝑏b are called associates.

    Divisibility relations are partial order relations on rings, while associate relations are equivalence relations on rings. From the perspective of ideals, 𝑎 ∣𝑏a∣b is equivalent to (𝑏) ⊆(𝑎)(b)⊆(a), and 𝑎a and 𝑏b being associates is equivalent to (𝑎) =(𝑏)(a)=(b). Therefore, when discussing elements in rings, we usually do not distinguish between associates. Similar to the integer case, the greatest common divisor of 𝑎a and 𝑏b in a commutative ring is defined as the greatest lower bound of {𝑎,𝑏}{a,b}.

    Greatest Common Divisor

    For a commutative ring 𝑅R and its elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R, if there exists a non-zero element 𝑑 ∈𝑅d∈R such that 𝑑 ∣𝑎d∣a and 𝑑 ∣𝑏d∣b, and for any 𝑑′d′ satisfying 𝑑′ ∣𝑎d′∣a and 𝑑′ ∣𝑏d′∣b, we have 𝑑′ ∣𝑑d′∣d, then 𝑑d is called the greatest common divisor of 𝑎a and 𝑏b, denoted gcd(𝑎,𝑏)gcd(a,b).

    In an integral domain, the greatest common divisor is uniquely determined up to associates. The discussion below is limited to integral domains.

    We can also establish the concept of prime numbers in integral domains. In number theory, prime numbers have two equivalent definitions, but in general integral domains, these two definitions correspond to different concepts:

    Prime Element

    Let an integral domain 𝑅R have a non-zero element 𝑝 ∈𝑅p∈R. If (𝑝)(p) is a prime ideal, that is, 𝑝p is not invertible, and 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑏p∣ab always implies 𝑝 ∣𝑎p∣a or 𝑝 ∣𝑏p∣b, then 𝑝p is called a prime element.

    Irreducible Element

    Let an integral domain 𝑅R have a non-zero element 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R. If 𝑟r is not invertible, and for any 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R with 𝑟 =𝑎𝑏r=ab, either 𝑎a or 𝑏b is invertible, then 𝑟r is called an irreducible element, or 𝑟r is irreducible. Conversely, if 𝑟 =𝑎𝑏r=ab and neither 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R are invertible, then 𝑟r is reducible.

    It can be shown that the principal ideal (𝑟)(r) generated by an irreducible element 𝑟r is always maximal among all principal ideals of the ring; however, in general integral domains, not all ideals are principal ideals, so the concepts of irreducible elements and maximal ideals are not equivalent.

    Similar to proving that prime ideals are always maximal in principal ideal domains, we can generally prove the following conclusion:

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be an integral domain. If 𝑎 ∈𝑅a∈R is a prime element, then 𝑎a is also an irreducible element.

    Proof

    Let 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R be a prime element, and 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R satisfy 𝑟 =𝑎𝑏r=ab. Since 𝑟r is a prime element, we can assume 𝑟 ∣𝑎r∣a holds, so 𝑎 =𝑐𝑟 =𝑐𝑏𝑎a=cr=cba. Since cancellation holds in integral domains, we have 1 =𝑏𝑐1=bc, so 𝑏b has an inverse 𝑐c. This shows that 𝑟r is irreducible.

    The converse does not hold.

    Counterexample

    In the quadratic integer ring 𝐙[√−5]Z[−5], 33 is irreducible, but 9 =3 ⋅3 =(2 +√−5)(2 −√−5)9=3⋅3=(2+−5)(2−−5), so it is not a prime element.

    Here is the proof of this counterexample. Readers unfamiliar with quadratic integer rings should first read the Quadratic Integer Rings section. Let 𝑁( ⋅)N(⋅) be the norm on the quadratic integer ring. For any factorization 3 =𝑎𝑏3=ab, we have 𝑁(𝑎)𝑁(𝑏) =𝑁(3) =9N(a)N(b)=N(3)=9. If 𝑎,𝑏a,b are not invertible, then both 𝑁(𝑎)N(a) and 𝑁(𝑏)N(b) are greater than 11, so necessarily 𝑁(𝑎) =𝑁(𝑏) =3N(a)=N(b)=3. However, there is no such element on 𝐙[√−5]Z[−5], i.e., 𝑥2 +5𝑦2 =3x2+5y2=3 has no integer solutions. This shows that 33 is irreducible. As for 33 not being a prime element, it is to prove that 33 cannot divide 2 ±√−52±−5, which is obvious.

    Euclidean Domains

    Related reading: (Extended) Euclidean Algorithm, Bézout's Theorem

    A Euclidean domain is an integral domain that allows Euclidean algorithm (i.e., division with remainder).

    Euclidean Domain

    For an integral domain 𝑅R, if there exists a map 𝑁 :𝑅 ∖{0} →𝐍N:R∖{0}→N such that for any 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R with 𝑏 ≠0b≠0, there exist 𝑞,𝑟 ∈𝑅q,r∈R such that 𝑎 =𝑞𝑏 +𝑟a=qb+r holds and either 𝑟 =0r=0 or 𝑁(𝑟) <𝑁(𝑏)N(r)<N(b), then 𝑅R is called a Euclidean domain. The map 𝑁N is called the norm of elements in the Euclidean domain.

    Other Equivalent Definitions

    The definition in this article only defines the norm at non-zero elements. Different texts may handle the definition of Euclidean domains differently. For example, some texts may additionally define 𝑁(0) =0N(0)=0; but since 𝑁(0)N(0) is not used in the subsequent division with remainder, this is not important. For another example, the definition in Wikipedia also requires that the norm 𝑁N satisfies: for any non-zero 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R, 𝑁(𝑎) ≤𝑁(𝑎𝑏)N(a)≤N(ab). However, it is easy to verify that if a Euclidean domain 𝑅R has a norm 𝑁( ⋅)N(⋅) satisfying the conditions in this article's definition, then we can define 𝑁′(𝑎) =min𝑏∈𝑅∖{0}𝑁(𝑎𝑏)N′(a)=minb∈R∖{0}N(ab) to make it satisfy the additional property 𝑁′(𝑎) ≤𝑁′(𝑎𝑏)N′(a)≤N′(ab). Therefore, these different definitions are equivalent.

    This definition is actually a generalization of division with remainder in integers. The existence of the norm allows measuring the relative size of the remainder and divisor. When performing Euclidean algorithm, the norm of the corresponding remainder is also decreasing; because the norm takes values in natural numbers, such a process must end at 𝑟 =0r=0. Thus, we obtain the Euclidean algorithm on Euclidean domains.

    Being able to perform Euclidean algorithm means that we can efficiently compute the greatest common divisor on Euclidean domains. Completely analogizing with integer divisibility theory, the result of Euclidean algorithm is always the greatest common divisor, and Bézout's theorem holds, where the coefficients can be determined by the extended Euclidean algorithm.

    Theorem

    For a Euclidean domain 𝑅R and its elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R, the result 𝑑d obtained by applying Euclidean algorithm to 𝑎a and 𝑏b is the greatest common divisor of 𝑎a and 𝑏b, and there exist 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝑅x,y∈R such that 𝑑 =𝑎𝑥 +𝑏𝑦d=ax+by holds; conversely, any element of the form 𝑎𝑥 +𝑏𝑦ax+by is a multiple of 𝑑d.

    Note that in the language of ring theory, all elements of the form 𝑎𝑥 +𝑏𝑦ax+by are precisely the elements in the ideal (𝑎,𝑏)(a,b), and this theorem shows that (𝑎,𝑏)(a,b) must be the principal ideal (𝑑)(d).

    In fact, ideals in Euclidean domains are always principal ideals.

    Theorem

    Ideals in Euclidean domains are always principal ideals.

    Proof

    Let 𝑅R be a Euclidean domain, and 𝐼I its ideal. If 𝐼 ={0}I={0}, it is obviously a principal ideal. Suppose 𝐼I is a non-zero ideal. By definition, 𝑅R has a norm 𝑁( ⋅)N(⋅), so we can take 𝑑d, a non-zero element in 𝐼I with minimal norm. Then for any 𝑎 ∈𝐼a∈I, we have 𝑎 =𝑞𝑑 +𝑟a=qd+r with 𝑟 =0r=0 or 𝑁(𝑟) <𝑁(𝑑)N(r)<N(d). Since 𝑟 =𝑎 −𝑞𝑑 ∈𝐼r=a−qd∈I, by the choice of 𝑑d, we know 𝑟 =0r=0, i.e., 𝑎 =𝑞𝑑 ∈(𝑑)a=qd∈(d). This shows that 𝐼I is necessarily a principal ideal.

    Principal Ideal Domains

    An integral domain where all ideals are principal ideals is called a principal ideal domain. This is a fairly well-behaved and quite common type of integral domain. In these rings, the concept of ideals in the ring is equivalent to the concept of multiples in integers.

    Principal Ideal Domain

    For an integral domain 𝑅R, if all its ideals are principal ideals, then it is called a principal ideal domain (PID).

    Thus, the last theorem in the previous section can be restated as:

    Theorem

    Euclidean domains are necessarily principal ideal domains.

    In principal ideal domains, maximal ideals are equivalent to ideals generated by irreducible elements. Similar to how prime numbers and irreducible elements are equivalent in integers, in principal ideal domains, these two concepts are also equivalent, so maximal ideals and prime ideals are also completely equivalent.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a principal ideal domain with non-zero ideal 𝐼I. Then 𝐼I is a prime ideal if and only if 𝐼I is a maximal ideal.

    Proof

    We only need to prove that prime ideals are maximal. Let (𝑝)(p) be a non-zero prime ideal in the principal ideal domain 𝑅R, and let (𝑎)(a) be an ideal satisfying (𝑝) ⊆(𝑎) ⊆𝑅(p)⊆(a)⊆R. This shows 𝑎 ∣𝑝a∣p, so there exists 𝑏 ∈𝑅b∈R such that 𝑝 =𝑎𝑏p=ab. But since (𝑝)(p) is a prime ideal, 𝑎𝑏 ∈(𝑝)ab∈(p) means 𝑎 ∈(𝑝)a∈(p) or 𝑏 ∈(𝑝)b∈(p). If 𝑎 ∈(𝑝)a∈(p), then (𝑎) ⊆(𝑝)(a)⊆(p), so (𝑎) =(𝑝)(a)=(p); if 𝑏 ∈(𝑝)b∈(p), then 𝑏 =𝑐𝑝b=cp, so 𝑝 =𝑎𝑐𝑝p=acp, and since 𝑝 ≠0p≠0, we have 1 =𝑎𝑐1=ac, i.e., 𝑎a has an inverse 𝑐c, so (𝑎) =𝑅(a)=R. This shows that (𝑝)(p) is a maximal ideal.

    Corollary

    Let 𝑅R be a principal ideal domain with non-zero element 𝑟r. Then 𝑟r is a prime element if and only if 𝑟r is irreducible.

    The analysis of Bézout's theorem in the previous section can be transferred to principal ideal domains.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a principal ideal domain, and 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R be non-zero elements. Let 𝑑 ∈𝑅d∈R be the generator of the ideal (𝑎,𝑏)(a,b). Then the greatest common divisor of 𝑎a and 𝑏b is 𝑑d, and it is uniquely determined up to associates; moreover, there exist 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝑅x,y∈R such that 𝑎𝑥 +𝑏𝑦 =𝑑ax+by=d holds.

    That is, Bézout's theorem still holds in principal ideal domains. Also, the existence of greatest common divisors, the main difference between Euclidean domains and principal ideal domains is that in the former, greatest common divisors can be computed efficiently through Euclidean algorithm, but in principal ideal domains, there is generally no such efficient algorithm.

    Unique Factorization Domains

    A more general concept than principal ideal domains is the unique factorization domain. The unique factorization theorem for integers is called the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. Similar unique factorization theorems actually hold in some integral domains that are not principal ideal domains. Such integral domains are called unique factorization domains.

    Unique Factorization Domain

    For an integral domain 𝑅R, if any non-zero and non-invertible element 𝑟r can be written as 𝑟 =𝑝1⋯𝑝𝑛r=p1⋯pn, where 𝑝1,⋯,𝑝𝑛p1,⋯,pn are possibly repeated irreducible elements, and such factorization is unique up to associates and rearrangement, then 𝑅R is called a unique factorization domain (UFD).

    The fundamental theorem of arithmetic shows that the integer ring 𝐙Z is a unique factorization domain.

    The previous section gave a counterexample where irreducible elements are not prime elements, and the integral domain 𝐙[√−5]Z[−5] involved does not satisfy unique factorization. However, in all unique factorization domains, irreducible elements and prime elements are both equivalent.

    Theorem

    For a unique factorization domain 𝑅R and its non-zero element 𝑎 ∈𝑅a∈R, 𝑎a is a prime element if and only if 𝑎a is irreducible.

    Proof

    We only need to prove that irreducible elements are prime elements. For an irreducible element 𝑟r, if 𝑟 ∣𝑎𝑏r∣ab, then there exists 𝑐 ∈𝑅c∈R such that 𝑎𝑏 =𝑟𝑐ab=rc holds. Since 𝑅R is a unique factorization domain, we can factor 𝑎,𝑏,𝑐 ∈𝑅a,b,c∈R into products of irreducible elements. Comparing both sides, from the uniqueness of factorization, 𝑟r must be associate with some irreducible factor of 𝑎a or 𝑏b. Hence, 𝑟r divides 𝑎a or 𝑏b. This shows that 𝑟r is also a prime element.

    All principal ideal domains are unique factorization domains.

    Theorem

    Principal ideal domains are necessarily unique factorization domains.

    Proof

    Let 𝑅R be a principal ideal domain, and 𝑟 ∈𝑅r∈R is neither zero nor invertible. To show that 𝑟r can be uniquely factored into a product of irreducible elements, we can do it in two steps: first prove existence of factorization, then prove uniqueness of factorization.

    The existence of factorization is quite natural. If 𝑟r is already irreducible, there is no need to continue factoring; otherwise, there must exist 𝑟1𝑟2r1r2 such that 𝑟 =𝑟1𝑟2r=r1r2 and neither 𝑟1r1 nor 𝑟2r2 are invertible. Furthermore, if 𝑟1r1 and 𝑟2r2 are both irreducible, then there is no need to continue factoring; otherwise, we can further factor those in 𝑟1r1 and 𝑟2r2 that are not irreducible, and 𝑟r can be written as a product of more elements. Thus, as long as not all factors in the product are irreducible, we can continue the factorization process. The factorization must terminate after finitely many steps. Otherwise, the axiom of choice guarantees that we can extract an infinite chain {𝑟(𝑖)}∞𝑖=0{r(i)}i=0∞ from 𝑅R satisfying 𝑟(0) =𝑟r(0)=r and 𝑟(𝑖+1) ∣𝑟(𝑖)r(i+1)∣r(i) for all 𝑖 ∈𝐍i∈N, and these divisibility relations are all strict, i.e., there are no associates in the chain. In the language of ideals, this corresponds to a strictly increasing infinite chain of ideals: 𝐼0 ⊂𝐼1 ⊂⋯ ⊂𝐼𝑖 ⊂⋯ ⊂𝑅I0⊂I1⊂⋯⊂Ii⊂⋯⊂R, where 𝐼𝑖 =(𝑟(𝑖))Ii=(r(i)). It is easy to verify that the union 𝐼 =⋃∞𝑖=0𝐼𝑖I=⋃i=0∞Ii is also an ideal, so it must be principal. Let 𝑎a be the generator of the principal ideal 𝐼I. Thus, there exists 𝑛 ∈𝐍n∈N such that 𝑎 ∈𝐼𝑛a∈In. So 𝐼 =(𝑎) ⊆𝐼𝑛I=(a)⊆In. This shows that such a strictly increasing infinite chain of ideals does not exist, so the factorization process must terminate after finitely many steps.

    Now we prove the uniqueness of factorization. We can do induction on the number of factors in the factorization. The key step in induction is to verify that if 𝑟 =𝑝1𝑝2⋯𝑝𝑛 =𝑞1𝑞2⋯𝑞𝑚r=p1p2⋯pn=q1q2⋯qm and 𝑛 ≤𝑚n≤m, then 𝑝1p1 must be associate with some 𝑞𝑗qj. Here we need to use the previous conclusion: in principal ideal domains, irreducible elements are all prime elements. Since 𝑝1p1 is irreducible in 𝑅R, it is also a prime element, so for the product on the right side, we can show by induction that there exists some element 𝑞𝑗qj such that 𝑝1 ∣𝑞𝑗p1∣qj. So there exists 𝑐 ∈𝑅c∈R such that 𝑞𝑗 =𝑝1𝑐qj=p1c, and since 𝑞𝑗qj is irreducible and 𝑝1p1 is also irreducible, by definition 𝑐c must be invertible, so 𝑝1p1 is associate with 𝑞𝑗qj. Then we can use the cancellation law to cancel 𝑝1p1 and 𝑞𝑗qj on both sides, and multiply the associate difference by one of the remaining elements. By the induction hypothesis, the number of irreducible elements in 𝑝2⋯𝑝𝑛p2⋯pn and 𝑞1⋯𝑞𝑗−1𝑞𝑗+1⋯𝑞𝑚q1⋯qj−1qj+1⋯qm must be equal, and they are the same up to associates. Theorem proved.

    Finally, the existence of greatest common divisors still holds on unique factorization domains.

    Theorem

    Let 𝑅R be a unique factorization domain with non-zero elements 𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝑅a,b∈R. Suppose they can be factored as 𝑎 =𝑢𝑝𝑟11⋯𝑝𝑟𝑛𝑛a=up1r1⋯pnrn and 𝑏 =𝑣𝑝𝑠11⋯𝑝𝑠𝑛𝑛b=vp1s1⋯pnsn, where 𝑢,𝑣u,v are invertible elements, 𝑝1,⋯,𝑝𝑛p1,⋯,pn are distinct irreducible elements, and 𝑟𝑖,𝑠𝑖ri,si are natural numbers. Then one greatest common divisor of them is 𝑑 =𝑝min{𝑟1,𝑠1}1⋯𝑝min{𝑟𝑛,𝑠𝑛}𝑛d=p1min{r1,s1}⋯pnmin{rn,sn}.

    This actually shows that the existence of greatest common divisors is a weaker condition than the unique factorization theorem2.

    Example: Quadratic Integer Rings

    Related reading: Quadratic Fields

    The understanding of abstract algebra cannot be separated from examples. It is precisely because the study of Fermat's Last Theorem required studying the properties of a type of algebraic integers that ring theory developed into what it is today3. Here we discuss the simplest algebraic integers, i.e., quadratic integers. Many proofs in this section require complex algebraic number theory knowledge, so they are omitted.

    A quadratic integer refers to the complex root of a quadratic equation 𝛼2 +𝑏𝛼 +𝑐 =0α2+bα+c=0 with integer coefficients and leading coefficient 1. All quadratic integers can and only can have the form

    𝛼=𝑎+𝑏𝜔, (𝑎,𝑏∈𝐙)α=a+bω, (a,b∈Z)

    where

    𝜔=⎧{ {⎨{ {⎩1+√𝐷2,𝐷≡1(mod4),√𝐷,𝐷≡2,3(mod4),ω={1+D2,D≡1(mod4),D,D≡2,3(mod4),

    and 𝐷D is square-free.

    Analysis

    According to the quadratic formula, the roots of this equation can definitely be written as

    𝛼=−𝑏±√𝑏2−4𝑐2.α=−b±b2−4c2.

    When 𝑏 =2𝑘 +1b=2k+1 is odd, this root can be written as

    𝛼=−𝑘−1±√4(𝑘2+𝑘−𝑐)+12.α=−k−1±4(k2+k−c)+12.

    Otherwise, when 𝑏 =2𝑘b=2k is even, this root can be written as

    𝛼=−𝑘±√𝑘2−𝑐.α=−k±k2−c.

    From this, we can conclude that quadratic integers must have the above form.

    It is easy to verify that for such 𝜔ω, the set 𝐙[𝜔] ={𝑎 +𝑏𝜔 :𝑎,𝑏 ∈𝐙}Z[ω]={a+bω:a,b∈Z} forms a ring. This is called the quadratic integer ring, and its fraction field is the quadratic field 𝐐(√𝐷)Q(D). When 𝐷 >0D>0, all quadratic integers are real numbers, so they are also called real quadratic integer rings; when 𝐷 <0D<0, quadratic integers other than integers are complex numbers, so they are also called imaginary quadratic integer rings.

    All quadratic integer rings 𝐙[𝜔]Z[ω] are integral domains. When 𝐷 = −1D=−1, 𝐙[√−1]Z[−1] (also denoted 𝐙[i]Z[i]) is also called the Gaussian integer ring; when 𝐷 = −3D=−3, 𝐙[1+√−32]Z[1+−32] is also called the Eisenstein integer ring.

    For a quadratic integer 𝑎 +𝑏𝜔a+bω, its conjugate can be defined as 𝑎 +𝑏¯𝜔a+bω¯, where

    ¯𝜔=⎧{ {⎨{ {⎩1−√𝐷2,𝐷≡1(mod4),−√𝐷,𝐷≡2,3(mod4),ω¯={1−D2,D≡1(mod4),−D,D≡2,3(mod4),

    Note that when 𝐷 >0D>0, quadratic integers are real numbers, so the concept of conjugate here is not exactly the same as the concept of conjugate for complex numbers, but they are both special cases of the concept of conjugate of algebraic elements in field theory. Conjugate quadratic integers are roots of the same quadratic equation with integer coefficients.

    The norm can be defined on quadratic integer rings

    $$

    \begin{aligned} N(a+b\omega)&=(a+b\omega)(a+b\bar\omega)\ &=\begin{cases} a2+ab+\dfrac{1-D}{4}b2,& D\equiv 1\pmod 4,\ a2-Db2,& D\equiv 2,3\pmod 4. \end{cases} \end{aligned} $$

    The norm of a quadratic integer is always an integer. Particularly, when 𝐷 <0D<0, the norm is always a natural number. The norm preserves multiplicative structure, i.e., 𝑁(𝑎𝑏) =𝑁(𝑎)𝑁(𝑏)N(ab)=N(a)N(b).

    The invertible elements (units) in quadratic integer rings can and only can be those elements with norm ±1±1. For the case 𝐷 >0D>0, this corresponds to considering solutions of the Pell equation 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±1x2−Dy2=±1 or 𝑥2 −𝐷𝑦2 = ±4x2−Dy2=±4. For the case 𝐷 <0D<0, it is easy to verify that except for the special cases where the invertible elements in the Gaussian integer ring 𝐙[i]Z[i] are { ±1, ±i}{±1,±i} and those in the Eisenstein integer ring 𝐙[𝜔]Z[ω] are { ±1, ±𝜔, ±𝜔2}{±1,±ω,±ω2}, in other cases, invertible elements are only { ±1}{±1}.

    The norm 𝑁(𝛼)N(α) defined on quadratic integer rings can be used to prove that they are Euclidean domains. For the case 𝐷 >0D>0, we need to use its absolute value |𝑁(𝛼)||N(α)| as the norm in the definition of Euclidean domain. Using this norm, it can be proved that when 𝐷 <0D<0,

    𝐷=−1,−2,−3,−7,−11D=−1,−2,−3,−7,−11

    or when 𝐷 >0D>0,

    𝐷=2,3,5,6,7,11,13,17,19,21,29,33,37,41,57,73D=2,3,5,6,7,11,13,17,19,21,29,33,37,41,57,73

    the corresponding quadratic integer rings are Euclidean domains under the norm |𝑁( ⋅)||N(⋅)|. However, the norm in the definition of Euclidean domains is not necessarily the norm defined above. For example, when 𝐷 =14,69D=14,69, the corresponding quadratic integer rings are also Euclidean domains, but other norms need to be used. For the case 𝐷 <0D<0, it can be proved that the cases given above are all Euclidean domains in quadratic integer rings.

    Using more complex methods, we can also determine whether a quadratic integer ring is a principal ideal domain. It can be proved that when 𝐷 <0D<0, only

    𝐷=−1,−2,−3,−7,−11,−19,−43,−67,−163D=−1,−2,−3,−7,−11,−19,−43,−67,−163

    corresponding quadratic integer rings are principal ideal domains. Comparing with the above results, we can see that cases like 𝐷 = −19D=−19 provide examples of principal ideal domains that are not Euclidean domains. For the case 𝐷 >0D>0, there are currently no complete results.

    However, it can be proved that in quadratic integer rings, unique factorization domains and principal ideal domains are equivalent. The above results show that, for example, 𝐙[√−5]Z[−5] is not a principal ideal domain, and therefore not a unique factorization domain. We have already actually proven through examples that it cannot be uniquely factored, i.e.,

    9=3×3=(2+√−5)×(2−√−5).9=3×3=(2+−5)×(2−−5).

    Using the same example, we can show that the ideal (3,2 +√5)(3,2+5) is also not principal. Later, we will see that a simple example of a unique factorization domain that is not a principal ideal domain is the polynomial ring 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x].

    Although many quadratic integer rings are not unique factorization domains, they are all Dedekind domains. This means that all non-trivial ideals in quadratic integer rings can be uniquely factored into products of prime ideals. However, if the quadratic integer ring itself is not a principal ideal domain, these prime ideal factors do not necessarily correspond to prime elements, so the unique factorization theorem (i.e., factoring numbers into products of primes) no longer holds: this is also the original motivation for studying ideals rather than numbers.

    Polynomial Rings

    Related reading: Introduction to Polynomial Techniques

    In competitive programming, various operations on polynomials are often encountered. Operations on polynomials such as multiplication, inversion, and remainder can be seen as generalizations of operations on numbers to polynomial rings. Using the language of abstract algebra, we can more quickly understand the properties of related operations on polynomial rings.

    Polynomial

    For a non-zero commutative unital ring 𝑅R, a polynomial over 𝑅R is a formal sum

    𝑛∑𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘=𝑎0+𝑎1𝑥+⋯+𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1+𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛,∑k=0nakxk=a0+a1x+⋯+an−1xn−1+anxn,

    where 𝑛 ∈𝐍n∈N, and for each 𝑘k, 𝑎𝑘 ∈𝑅ak∈R. These 𝑎𝑘ak are called the coefficients of the polynomial, and the corresponding 𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘akxk is called a term of the polynomial. The 𝑘k in the term 𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘akxk is called the degree of that term.

    Polynomials where all coefficients are zero (i.e., the zero element) are called zero polynomials, denoted 00. For other polynomials, let 𝑎𝑛 ≠0an≠0, i.e., 𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛anxn is the term with the highest degree among terms with non-zero coefficients. At this time, the natural number 𝑛n is called the degree of the polynomial, and its term 𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛anxn is called the leading term, and 𝑎𝑛an is also called the leading coefficient. A polynomial whose leading coefficient is one (i.e., the unity element) is called a monic polynomial. The degree of the zero polynomial is not specified, or defined as −∞−∞.

    The 𝑥x appearing in polynomial notation is called the indeterminate of the polynomial. It has no meaning itself and has no range of values. Its existence is only to mark the position of coefficients through its exponent. Therefore, polynomials can also be written as sequences over 𝑅R

    (𝑎0,𝑎1,...,𝑎𝑛−1,𝑎𝑛,0,0,⋯).(a0,a1,...,an−1,an,0,0,⋯).

    However, such sequences can only have finitely many non-zero terms. If two polynomials have the same coefficient sequence, they are said to be equal. This is equivalent to their formal sums being completely identical after complementing zero coefficients. Below, we will no longer distinguish the notation of formal sums of equal polynomials: readers can complement the missing zero coefficients themselves if needed.

    Sometimes we need to substitute elements of the ring into the indeterminate of polynomials. For example, let 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) be a polynomial in 𝑅R and 𝑎 ∈𝑅a∈R, then substituting 𝑎a into 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) gives 𝑓(𝑎)f(a). Its meaning is: in the formal sum of the polynomial, replacing 𝑥x with 𝑎a, we get an arithmetic expression in 𝑅R, and 𝑓(𝑎)f(a) is the result of this expression in 𝑅R.

    "Polynomial" and "Polynomial Function"

    Readers should not confuse these two concepts. Polynomials are only finite-length coefficient sequences, and they do not automatically become functions. Although the operation of substituting ring elements into indeterminates does map polynomials to polynomial functions, such a mapping is not necessarily injective. For example, as a polynomial over 𝐅𝑝Fp, 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑥𝑝 −𝑥f(x)=xp−x is obviously not equal to the zero polynomial; but as a polynomial function 𝐅𝑝 →𝐅𝑝Fp→Fp, it is always equal to zero (i.e., Fermat's little theorem). Although the two concepts are different, many concepts of polynomial functions can be generalized to polynomials, for example, we can define the (formal) derivative, indefinite integral, composition of polynomials by analogy with differentiation, indefinite integration, and composition of polynomial functions. These formal operations do not depend on any topological structure, but many operation rules still hold.

    For polynomials

    $$

    \begin{aligned} f(x)&=a_0+a_1x+\cdots+a_{n-1}x{n-1}+a_nxn,\ g(x)&=b_0+b_1x+\cdots+b_{n-1}x{n-1}+b_nxn, \end{aligned} $$

    the addition of polynomials is defined as

    𝑓(𝑥)+𝑔(𝑥)=(𝑎0+𝑏0)+(𝑎1+𝑏1)𝑥+⋯+(𝑎𝑛−1+𝑏𝑛−1)𝑥𝑛−1+(𝑎𝑛+𝑏𝑛)𝑥𝑛,f(x)+g(x)=(a0+b0)+(a1+b1)x+⋯+(an−1+bn−1)xn−1+(an+bn)xn,

    and the multiplication of polynomials is defined as

    𝑓(𝑥)𝑔(𝑥)=𝑎0𝑏0+(𝑎1𝑏0+𝑎0𝑏1)𝑥+(𝑎2𝑏0+𝑎1𝑏1+𝑎0𝑏2)𝑥2+⋯,f(x)g(x)=a0b0+(a1b0+a0b1)x+(a2b0+a1b1+a0b2)x2+⋯,

    where the coefficient of 𝑥𝑘xk is ∑𝑘𝑖=0𝑎𝑘−𝑖𝑏𝑖∑i=0kak−ibi. Under the addition and multiplication defined this way, the set of all polynomials over 𝑅R forms a ring, denoted 𝑅[𝑥]R[x].

    The degree of a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is denoted deg⁡𝑓(𝑥)deg⁡f(x). Polynomials with degree zero are constant polynomials, and along with the zero polynomial, they correspond to the embedding of 𝑅R in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]. Obviously, 𝑅R has zero divisors if and only if 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] has zero divisors.

    Theorem

    The polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] is an integral domain if and only if 𝑅R is an integral domain.

    On the polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] over an integral domain 𝑅R, the results of addition and multiplication satisfy

    $$

    \begin{aligned} \deg(f(x)+g(x)) &\le \max{\deg f(x),\deg g(x)},\ \deg(f(x)g(x)) &= \deg f(x) + \deg g(x). \end{aligned} $$

    Here we set deg⁡0 = −∞deg⁡0=−∞. Therefore, invertible elements in polynomial rings must also be those invertible elements in their constant polynomials. Any polynomial of degree one or higher is not invertible.

    The discussion below will be limited to polynomials over integral domains.

    Convention

    Below, we will not distinguish between "polynomials over ring 𝑅R" and "polynomials in polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]". For example, a polynomial being irreducible over ring 𝑅R means it is irreducible in ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]. Moreover, if 𝑅R is a subring of 𝑆S, then polynomials over 𝑅R automatically become polynomials over 𝑆S; we will not repeat this.

    Polynomial Rings over Fields

    Among polynomial rings over integral domains, the simplest are polynomial rings over fields. Polynomial ring over a field 𝐹F is 𝐹[𝑥]F[x]. Since coefficients can be divided, we can define division with remainder. Let the norm of a non-zero polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) be 𝑁(𝑓(𝑥)) =deg⁡𝑓(𝑥)N(f(x))=deg⁡f(x). Then for polynomials 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and non-zero polynomial 𝑔(𝑥)g(x) in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x], we can obviously perform division with remainder

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑔(𝑥)𝑞(𝑥)+𝑟(𝑥),f(x)=g(x)q(x)+r(x),

    where 𝑞(𝑥),𝑟(𝑥) ∈𝐹[𝑥]q(x),r(x)∈F[x], and 𝑟(𝑥) =0r(x)=0 or deg⁡𝑟(𝑥) <deg⁡𝑔(𝑥)deg⁡r(x)<deg⁡g(x). This shows that polynomial rings over fields are all Euclidean domains.

    Theorem

    The polynomial ring 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] over a field 𝐹F is a Euclidean domain, a principal ideal domain, and a unique factorization domain.

    In competitive programming, due to calculation precision reasons, we often consider the polynomial ring 𝐅𝑝[𝑥] =(𝐙/𝑝𝐙)[𝑥]Fp[x]=(Z/pZ)[x], where the modulus 𝑝p is required to be prime. Such rings allow operations like Euclidean algorithm. However, polynomial rings (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)[𝑥](Z/nZ)[x] corresponding to arbitrary modulus 𝑛n are not even integral domains.

    The fact that division with remainder holds means that polynomial roots always correspond to one factor of degree one.

    Root

    A root of a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is an element 𝜉 ∈𝐹ξ∈F such that 𝑓(𝜉) =0f(ξ)=0.

    Theorem

    For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F and an element 𝜉 ∈𝐹ξ∈F, 𝜉ξ is a root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) if and only if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) has a factor of degree one (𝑥 −𝜉)(x−ξ).

    Proof

    Division with remainder shows there exist 𝑞(𝑥),𝑟(𝑥)q(x),r(x) such that 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑞(𝑥)(𝑥 −𝜉) +𝑟(𝑥)f(x)=q(x)(x−ξ)+r(x) and deg⁡𝑟(𝑥) <deg⁡(𝑥 −𝜉) =1deg⁡r(x)<deg⁡(x−ξ)=1. Thus, 𝑟(𝑥)r(x) is a constant polynomial or zero polynomial, let 𝑟(𝑥) =𝑐r(x)=c, then we must have 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑞(𝑥)(𝑥 −𝜉) +𝑐f(x)=q(x)(x−ξ)+c. Substituting 𝑥 =𝜉x=ξ, hence 0 =𝑎(𝜉) =𝑐0=a(ξ)=c, i.e., 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑞(𝑥)(𝑥 −𝜉)f(x)=q(x)(x−ξ).

    The concept of roots can be generalized to multiple roots.

    Multiple Root

    If a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) has a factor (𝑥 −𝜉)𝑘(x−ξ)k, and (𝑥 −𝜉)𝑘+1(x−ξ)k+1 does not divide 𝑓(𝑥)f(x), then 𝜉ξ is called a 𝑘k-fold root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x). If 𝑘 >1k>1, then 𝜉ξ is called a multiple root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x); if 𝑘 =1k=1, then 𝜉ξ is called a simple root of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x).

    Theorem

    If a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over a field 𝐹F has (possibly repeated) roots 𝜉1,⋯,𝜉𝑘ξ1,⋯,ξk, then it must have the factor (𝑥 −𝜉1)⋯(𝑥 −𝜉𝑘)(x−ξ1)⋯(x−ξk). Furthermore, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over field 𝐹F has degree 𝑛n, then it has at most 𝑛n roots (counting multiplicities).

    Proof

    Note that 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] is a unique factorization domain.

    Although unique factorization holds for polynomials over fields, there is no general method to determine whether a given polynomial is reducible. Relatively small degrees are easier. For example, all linear polynomials are irreducible polynomials. On special fields where all irreducible polynomials are linear, such fields are called algebraically closed fields. On such fields, all polynomials that are not identically equal to non-zero constants have roots, so any polynomial of degree greater than one can be further factored. An example of such a field is the complex field 𝐂C. On the real field 𝐑R, there exist irreducible polynomials of degree two; on the rational field 𝐐Q, the structure of irreducible polynomials is more complex. The Field Theory page has more discussions on polynomials over rational fields and finite fields.

    The above conclusions are all about polynomials over fields. For polynomials over more general integral domains, they can often be transformed to such cases.

    Now consider the polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] over a unique factorization domain 𝑅R. Directly performing operations in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x], because coefficients often cannot be divided, many operations are limited. Consider extending 𝑅R to its fraction field 𝐹F, then consider factoring the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x]. Since 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] is known to be a unique factorization domain, we can reverse the factorization in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] to get the factorization in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]. Fortunately, such an approach is always possible.

    Gauss's Lemma

    For a unique factorization domain 𝑅R and its fraction field 𝐹F, if 𝑓(𝑥) ∈𝑅[𝑥]f(x)∈R[x] and in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] we have 𝑓(𝑥) =𝐴(𝑥)𝐵(𝑥)f(x)=A(x)B(x), then there exist 𝑠,𝑡 ∈𝐹s,t∈F such that 𝑎(𝑥) =𝑠𝐴(𝑥) ∈𝑅[𝑥]a(x)=sA(x)∈R[x], 𝑏(𝑥) =𝑡𝐵(𝑥) ∈𝑅[𝑥]b(x)=tB(x)∈R[x], and 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑎(𝑥)𝑏(𝑥)f(x)=a(x)b(x). Therefore, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x], then it is also irreducible in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x].

    Proof

    Let 𝑓(𝑥) ∈𝑅[𝑥]f(x)∈R[x] be reducible in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x], and 𝑓(𝑥) =𝐴(𝑥)𝐵(𝑥)f(x)=A(x)B(x). Let 𝑟𝑎ra and 𝑟𝑏rb be the least common multiples of the denominators of all coefficients in 𝐴(𝑥)A(x) and 𝐵(𝑥)B(x) respectively. Then ˜𝑎(𝑥) =𝑟𝑎𝐴(𝑥)a~(x)=raA(x) and ˜𝑏(𝑥) =𝑟𝑏𝐵(𝑥)b~(x)=rbB(x) are both polynomials over 𝑅R. Let 𝑟 =𝑟𝑎𝑟𝑏r=rarb, then 𝑟𝑓(𝑥) =˜𝑎(𝑥)˜𝑏(𝑥)rf(x)=a~(x)b~(x). If 𝑟r is an invertible element in 𝑅R, we can take the factorization 𝑓(𝑥) =(𝑟−1˜𝑎(𝑥))˜𝑏(𝑥)f(x)=(r−1a~(x))b~(x), which obviously satisfies the requirements of the lemma.

    Otherwise, if 𝑟r contains an irreducible element factor 𝑝p, we need to prove that we can cancel this factor on both sides, and ensure all coefficients remain in the integral domain 𝑅R. Note that 𝑝p must also be a prime element, so (𝑝)(p) is a prime ideal. Taking both sides modulo 𝑝p, we get the polynomial 0 =¯𝑎(𝑥)¯𝑏(𝑥)0=a¯(x)b¯(x) over (𝑅/(𝑝))[𝑥](R/(p))[x], where ¯𝑎a¯ and ¯𝑏b¯ are the polynomials after taking modulo 𝑝p. Since 𝑅/(𝑝)R/(p) is an integral domain, (𝑅/(𝑝))[𝑥](R/(p))[x] is also an integral domain, so we can assume ¯𝑎(𝑥) =0a¯(x)=0. This shows that all coefficients of ˜𝑎(𝑥)a~(x) are divisible by 𝑝p. Therefore, we can directly cancel the factor 𝑝p on both sides.

    According to the definition of unique factorization domain, 𝑟r has only finitely many such irreducible element factors, so after canceling them finitely many times, we transform to the case where 𝑟r is an invertible element in 𝑅R. The lemma is thus proved.

    Corollary

    For a unique factorization domain 𝑅R and its fraction field 𝐹F, if 𝑓(𝑥) ∈𝑅[𝑥]f(x)∈R[x] and all non-zero coefficients of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) are coprime (i.e., the greatest common divisor is the unity element of 𝑅R), then 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible in 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] if and only if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x].

    That is, irreducible elements in the polynomial ring 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x] are all irreducible in 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x]. An effective method to determine whether a polynomial with integer coefficients is irreducible is the Eisenstein criterion. According to Gauss's lemma, it also provides a method to determine whether polynomials with rational coefficients are irreducible.

    Eisenstein Criterion

    Let 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑎0 +𝑎1𝑥 +⋯ +𝑎𝑛−1𝑥𝑛−1 +𝑎𝑛𝑥𝑛f(x)=a0+a1x+⋯+an−1xn−1+anxn be a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree 𝑛n. If there exists a prime 𝑝p such that 𝑝 ∣𝑎𝑖p∣ai for all 𝑖 =0,1,⋯,𝑛 −1i=0,1,⋯,n−1, and 𝑝p does not divide 𝑎𝑛an, and 𝑝2p2 does not divide 𝑎0a0, then the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is irreducible over the rational field 𝐐Q. If gcd(𝑎0,𝑎1,⋯,𝑎𝑛) =1gcd(a0,a1,⋯,an)=1, then the polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is also irreducible over the integer ring 𝐙Z.

    Proof

    Using Gauss's lemma, if 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) is reducible over the rational field 𝐐Q, then it is also reducible over the integer ring 𝐙Z. Let 𝑓(𝑥) =𝑏(𝑥)𝑐(𝑥)f(x)=b(x)c(x) be its factorization in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x]. Taking both sides modulo prime 𝑝p, we get the factorization ――𝑓(𝑥) =――𝑏(𝑥)――𝑐(𝑥)f―(x)=b―(x)c―(x) in 𝐅𝑝[𝑥]Fp[x]. But the condition of the theorem shows that ――𝑓(𝑥) =𝑥𝑛f―(x)=xn, so there must exist integers 𝑚m such that ――𝑏(𝑥) =𝑥𝑚b―(x)=xm and ――𝑐(𝑥) =𝑥𝑛−𝑚c―(x)=xn−m, where 0 <𝑚 <𝑛0<m<n. Therefore, the constant terms 𝑏0b0 and 𝑐0c0 of 𝑏(𝑥)b(x) and 𝑐(𝑥)c(x) are both multiples of 𝑝p. Hence, the constant term 𝑎0 =𝑏0𝑐0a0=b0c0 of 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) must be a multiple of 𝑝2p2. This contradicts the given condition.

    Examples
    1. The polynomial 𝑥3 −2x3−2 is irreducible in 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x]. Applying the Eisenstein criterion with 𝑝 =2p=2 suffices.
    2. The polynomial 𝑥4 +1x4+1 is irreducible in 𝐐[𝑥]Q[x]. Otherwise, (𝑥 +1)4 +1 =𝑥4 +4𝑥3 +6𝑥2 +4𝑥 +2(x+1)4+1=x4+4x3+6x2+4x+2 would also be reducible. However, applying the Eisenstein criterion with 𝑝 =2p=2 shows that the latter is not irreducible.

    For a unique factorization domain 𝑅R, since the polynomial ring over its fraction field 𝐹F is a unique factorization domain, and Gauss's lemma shows that factorizations in 𝐹[𝑥]F[x] and 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] correspond to each other, 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] is also a unique factorization domain. Therefore, we have:

    Theorem

    The polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] is a unique factorization domain if and only if 𝑅R is a unique factorization domain.

    Here, 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x] provides an example that a unique factorization domain is not necessarily a principal ideal domain. For example, in 𝐙[𝑥]Z[x], (2,𝑥)(2,x) is not a principal ideal.

    There are many ways to extend polynomial rings. For example, for a polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x] over an integral domain 𝑅R, we can extend it to its fraction field, denoted 𝑅(𝑥)R(x). This fraction field is often called the field of rational fractions, where the basic form of elements is 𝑓(𝑥)𝑔(𝑥)f(x)g(x), where both 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) and 𝑔(𝑥)g(x) are polynomials.

    Multivariate Polynomial Rings

    Polynomial rings can be extended to cases with multiple indeterminates. For a commutative unital ring 𝑅R, we can define the polynomial ring over 𝑅R, i.e., the univariate polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]. Then we can define the polynomial ring over 𝑅[𝑥]R[x], i.e., 𝑅[𝑥][𝑦]R[x][y], which can be seen as the bivariate polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥,𝑦]R[x,y] over 𝑅R. From this, we can inductively define the 𝑘k-variate polynomial ring 𝑅[𝑥1,⋯,𝑥𝑘]R[x1,⋯,xk] over 𝑅R. When 𝑅R is an integral domain, any multivariate polynomial ring over 𝑅R is an integral domain; similarly, the property of unique factorization domains can also be transferred to any multivariate polynomial ring.

    Formal Power Series Rings

    We can also consider cases where formal sums can have arbitrarily many non-zero coefficients. A formal power series over a commutative unital ring 𝑅R is defined as

    ∞∑𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘=𝑎0+𝑎1𝑥+𝑎2𝑥2+⋯.∑k=0∞akxk=a0+a1x+a2x2+⋯.

    Addition and multiplication between power series can be defined in the same way as for polynomial rings 𝑅[𝑥]R[x]. Moreover, formal power series also form a ring, denoted 𝑅[[𝑥]]R[[x]]. Here, formal power series do not consider convergence or divergence, because each formal power series is actually just its coefficient sequence, and no more topological structure is given.

    The structure of formal power series rings is interesting. In polynomial rings over integral domains, invertible elements can only be constants. However, in formal power series rings, we can have

    (1−𝑥)−1=∞∑𝑘=0𝑥𝑘=1+𝑥+𝑥2+⋯.(1−x)−1=∑k=0∞xk=1+x+x2+⋯.

    This phenomenon is universal. As long as the constant term 𝑎0a0 of a formal power series is an invertible element in 𝑅R, then ∑∞𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘∑k=0∞akxk is also invertible. This is because if we set

    (∞∑𝑘=0𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘)(∞∑𝑘=0𝑏𝑘𝑥𝑘)=1,(∑k=0∞akxk)(∑k=0∞bkxk)=1,

    then by listing the equations that coefficients need to satisfy, we can recursively find expressions for 𝑏𝑘bk that involve only the inverse of 𝑎0a0.

    Various operations can be defined on formal power series rings, such as inversion, division, compositional inverse, formal derivatives, elementary functions, etc. See Introduction to Polynomial Techniques for details.

    Formal Laurent Series Rings

    Formal power series rings can be further extended to allow terms with negative degrees. A formal Laurent series over a commutative unital ring 𝑅R is defined as

    ∞∑𝑘=𝑁𝑎𝑘𝑥𝑘,∑k=N∞akxk,

    where 𝑁 ∈𝐙N∈Z. Therefore, formal Laurent series can have finitely many negative degree terms. Extending the previous addition and multiplication to formal Laurent series gives the formal Laurent series ring, denoted 𝑅((𝑥))R((x)). If 𝐹F is a field, then 𝐹((𝑥))F((x)) is also a field.

    Formal Laurent series rings have applications in Lagrange Inversion.

    Chinese Remainder Theorem

    Related reading: Chinese Remainder Theorem

    In number theory, the Chinese remainder theorem is often used to solve systems of number theory equations. For general commutative unital rings, we can also establish the Chinese remainder theorem. Each congruence equation is equivalent to specifying the image of the unknown in some quotient ring. Therefore, the Chinese remainder theorem in commutative unital rings is equivalent to determining elements in the ring through these images in quotient rings.

    This discussion can be transformed into formal language. For a non-zero commutative unital ring 𝑅R and its ideals 𝐼1,⋯,𝐼𝑛I1,⋯,In, consider the ring homomorphism 𝜑 :𝑅 →𝑅/𝐼1 ×⋯𝑅/𝐼𝑛φ:R→R/I1×⋯R/In, which maps 𝑟r to (𝑟 +𝐼1,⋯,𝑟 +𝐼𝑛)(r+I1,⋯,r+In). Here, 𝑟 +𝐼𝑖r+Ii is a coset, and ×× denotes the direct product of rings:

    Direct Product

    For rings 𝑅1R1 and 𝑅2R2, the direct product of their additive groups 𝑅1 ×𝑅2R1×R2 can define multiplication by multiplying each component separately, then 𝑅1 ×𝑅2R1×R2 becomes a ring, called the direct product of rings 𝑅1R1 and 𝑅2R2, still denoted 𝑅1 ×𝑅2R1×R2.

    The kernel of the homomorphism 𝜑φ is ker⁡𝜑 =𝐼1 ∩⋯ ∩𝐼𝑛ker⁡φ=I1∩⋯∩In. The question the Chinese remainder theorem needs to answer is under what conditions this map is surjective.

    In the case of number theory, the theorem requires these moduli to be coprime. This condition can be generalized to the case of ring theory.

    Coprime

    Let a ring 𝑅R have ideals 𝐼I and 𝐽J. If 𝐼 +𝐽 =𝑅I+J=R, then 𝐼I and 𝐽J are called comaximal.

    For the case of unital rings, if we consider principal ideals (𝑎)(a) and (𝑏)(b), this condition is equivalent to the existence of 𝑥,𝑦 ∈𝑅x,y∈R such that 𝑎𝑥 +𝑏𝑦 =1ax+by=1, which is similar to Bézout's theorem when integers are coprime. Using this definition, we can completely analogize the case of integer rings to establish the Chinese Remainder Theorem for commutative unital rings.

    Chinese Remainder Theorem

    Let a non-zero commutative unital ring 𝑅R have ideals 𝐼1,⋯,𝐼𝑛I1,⋯,In. If they are pairwise comaximal, then the ring homomorphism 𝜑φ defined above is surjective, its kernel equals the product of these ideals ker⁡𝜑 =𝐼1 ∩⋯ ∩𝐼𝑛 =𝐼1⋯𝐼𝑛ker⁡φ=I1∩⋯∩In=I1⋯In, therefore

    𝑅/(𝐼1⋯𝐼𝑛)=𝑅/(𝐼1∩⋯∩𝐼𝑛)≅𝑅/𝐼1×⋯×𝑅/𝐼𝑛.R/(I1⋯In)=R/(I1∩⋯∩In)≅R/I1×⋯×R/In.
    Proof

    The theorem is rich in content, but the conclusions that still need proof are only two: 𝜑φ is surjective and 𝐼1 ∩⋯ ∩𝐼𝑛 =𝐼1⋯𝐼𝑛I1∩⋯∩In=I1⋯In. The key is to make good use of the comaximal condition.

    First prove the case 𝑛 =2n=2. Since ideals 𝐼1I1 and 𝐼2I2 are comaximal, i.e., 𝐼1 +𝐼2 =𝑅I1+I2=R, the unity element 11 in 𝑅R can be written in the form 𝑎1 +𝑎2a1+a2 where 𝑎𝑖 ∈𝐼𝑖ai∈Ii. Since 𝑎1 ∈𝐼1a1∈I1 and 𝑎1 =1 −𝑎2 ∈1 +𝐼2a1=1−a2∈1+I2, we have 𝜑(𝑎1) =(𝐼1,1 +𝐼2)φ(a1)=(I1,1+I2); similarly, 𝜑(𝑎2) =(1 +𝐼1,𝐼2)φ(a2)=(1+I1,I2). Therefore, (𝜑(𝑎2),𝜑(𝑎1))(φ(a2),φ(a1)) plays a role similar to a "basis" in vector spaces. Therefore, for any image (𝑟1 +𝐼1,𝑟2 +𝐼2)(r1+I1,r2+I2), we can find the preimage 𝑟1𝑎2 +𝑟2𝑎1r1a2+r2a1 under the homomorphism 𝜑φ. This shows that 𝜑φ is surjective.

    We also need to prove 𝐼1 ∩𝐼2 =𝐼1𝐼2I1∩I2=I1I2. For general rings, 𝐼1𝐼2 ⊆𝐼1 ∩𝐼2I1I2⊆I1∩I2 always holds, and the key is the other direction. For any 𝑟 ∈𝐼1 ∩𝐼2r∈I1∩I2, we have 𝑟 =𝑟(𝑎1 +𝑎2) =𝑟𝑎1 +𝑟𝑎2 ∈𝐼1𝐼2r=r(a1+a2)=ra1+ra2∈I1I2. Therefore, 𝐼1 ∩𝐼2 ⊆𝐼1𝐼2I1∩I2⊆I1I2 also holds. This is what we needed to prove.

    For the case 𝑛 >2n>2, we need to use mathematical induction. The key step in induction is to prove that for pairwise comaximal ideals 𝐼1,⋯,𝐼𝑛I1,⋯,In, the ideal 𝐼1I1 and 𝐼2⋯𝐼𝑛I2⋯In are always comaximal. Since 𝐼1I1 is comaximal with each of 𝐼2,⋯,𝐼𝑛I2,⋯,In, for each 𝑖 =2,⋯,𝑛i=2,⋯,n, there exist 𝑎𝑖 ∈𝐼1ai∈I1 and 𝑏𝑖 ∈𝐼𝑖bi∈Ii such that 1 =𝑎𝑖 +𝑏𝑖1=ai+bi holds. Therefore, 1 =(𝑎2 +𝑏2)⋯(𝑎𝑛 +𝑏𝑛)1=(a2+b2)⋯(an+bn) holds. So, 1 ∈(𝑏2⋯𝑏𝑛) +𝐼1 ⊆𝐼1 +(𝐼2⋯𝐼𝑛)1∈(b2⋯bn)+I1⊆I1+(I2⋯In). This shows that the ideal 𝐼1I1 and 𝐼2⋯𝐼𝑛I2⋯In are comaximal.

    Application: Lagrange Interpolation Formula

    Related reading: Lagrange Interpolation, Fast Polynomial Interpolation

    The interpolation problem is: given a series of points {(𝑥𝑖,𝑦𝑖)}𝑛𝑖=1{(xi,yi)}i=1n, find a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over field 𝐹F such that 𝑓(𝑥𝑖) =𝑦𝑖f(xi)=yi holds for all 𝑖 =1,⋯,𝑛i=1,⋯,n. Of course, we assume all 𝑥𝑖xi are distinct. The Lagrange interpolation formula gives the general solution to such problems.

    For a polynomial 𝑓(𝑥)f(x) over field 𝐹F, the condition 𝑓(𝑥𝑖) =𝑦𝑖f(xi)=yi is equivalent to 𝑥𝑖xi being a root of 𝑓(𝑥) −𝑦𝑖f(x)−yi, hence equivalent to (𝑥 −𝑥𝑖) ∣(𝑓(𝑥) −𝑦𝑖)(x−xi)∣(f(x)−yi), i.e., 𝑓(𝑥) ≡𝑦𝑖(mod𝑥 −𝑥𝑖)f(x)≡yi(modx−xi). Therefore, the interpolation problem is equivalent to solving the system of congruence equations

    ⎧{ { {⎨{ { {⎩𝑓(𝑥)≡𝑦1(mod𝑥−𝑥1),𝑓(𝑥)≡𝑦2(mod𝑥−𝑥2),⋯𝑓(𝑥)≡𝑦𝑛(mod𝑥−𝑥𝑛).{f(x)≡y1(modx−x1),f(x)≡y2(modx−x2),⋯f(x)≡yn(modx−xn).

    These linear polynomials {𝑥 −𝑥𝑖}𝑛𝑖=1{x−xi}i=1n are pairwise coprime. According to the Chinese remainder theorem, the solution should have the form

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑦𝑖𝑀𝑖(𝑥),f(x)=∑i=1nyiMi(x),

    where 𝑀𝑖(𝑥) =𝑚𝑖(𝑥)∏𝑗≠𝑖(𝑥 −𝑥𝑗)Mi(x)=mi(x)∏j≠i(x−xj) and 𝑀𝑖(𝑥) ≡1(mod𝑥 −𝑥𝑖)Mi(x)≡1(modx−xi). According to the equivalence derived earlier, this is equivalent to 𝑀𝑖(𝑥𝑖) =1Mi(xi)=1, i.e.,

    𝑚𝑖(𝑥𝑖)∏𝑗≠𝑖(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗)=1.mi(xi)∏j≠i(xi−xj)=1.

    We can take 𝑚𝑖(𝑥)mi(x) to be a constant polynomial, i.e.,

    𝑚𝑖(𝑥)=1∏𝑗≠𝑖(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗).mi(x)=1∏j≠i(xi−xj).

    From this, we get the Lagrange interpolation formula

    𝑓(𝑥)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑦𝑖∏𝑗≠𝑖(𝑥−𝑥𝑗)∏𝑗≠𝑖(𝑥𝑖−𝑥𝑗).f(x)=∑i=1nyi∏j≠i(x−xj)∏j≠i(xi−xj).

    In general, extending this method can also derive the Hermite interpolation formula, which allows restricting the values of certain derivatives of polynomials at points.

    Application: Multiplicative Group of Integer Congruence Classes

    Related reading: Primitive Roots, Fundamental Theorem of Finitely Generated Abelian Groups

    As an application of the Chinese remainder theorem and related content of group theory, this section discusses the structure of the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n. This section omits the overline notation for congruence classes.

    The multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n refers to (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)×, i.e., the multiplicative group of invertible elements in the quotient ring 𝐙/𝑛𝐙Z/nZ (also called the group of units). The order of the group (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)× is 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n), because the necessary and sufficient condition for invertibility is coprime with 𝑛n. Here, 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) is the Euler totient function. Moreover, the group (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)× is always an abelian group.

    According to the fundamental theorem of arithmetic, modulus 𝑛n can be factored into the product of powers of distinct primes:

    𝑛=𝑝𝛼11⋯𝑝𝛼𝑠𝑠.n=p1α1⋯psαs.

    It is easy to verify that for ideals in the integer ring, the condition that ideals are comaximal is equivalent to the condition that their generators are coprime. Therefore, applying the Chinese remainder theorem gives

    $$

    \mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z\cong\mathbf Z/p_1^{\alpha_1}\mathbf Z\times\cdots\times\mathbf Z/p_s^{\alpha_s}\mathbf Z. $$

    Ring isomorphism implies corresponding multiplicative structures are also isomorphic, so

    $$

    (\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z)^\times\cong(\mathbf Z/p_1^{\alpha_1}\mathbf Z)^\times\times\cdots\times(\mathbf Z/p_s^{\alpha_s}\mathbf Z)^\times. $$

    This shows that 𝜑(𝑛) =𝜑(𝑝𝛼11)⋯𝜑(𝑝𝛼𝑛𝑛)φ(n)=φ(p1α1)⋯φ(pnαn), i.e., the Euler function is a multiplicative function.

    Therefore, to study the general case, we only need to consider the case where the modulus is a prime power 𝑝𝑘pk. For the case of prime powers, we need to consider separately the two cases of 𝑝 =2p=2 and 𝑝p being an odd prime:

    • For the case 𝑝 =2p=2, direct verification shows (𝐙/2𝐙)× ≅𝐶1(Z/2Z)×≅C1 and (𝐙/4𝐙)× ≅𝐶2(Z/4Z)×≅C2. For 𝑘 ≥3k≥3, we have (𝐙/2𝑘𝐙)× ≅𝐶2 ×𝐶2𝑘−2(Z/2kZ)×≅C2×C2k−2.

      Proof

      Using the binomial theorem, direct calculation shows

      52𝑘−2=(1+22)2𝑘−2≡1(mod2𝑘),52𝑘−3=(1+22)2𝑘−3≡1+2𝑘−1(mod2𝑘).52k−2=(1+22)2k−2≡1(mod2k),52k−3=(1+22)2k−3≡1+2k−1(mod2k).

      So, 55 is an element of order 2𝑘−22k−2 in (𝐙/2𝑘𝐙)×(Z/2kZ)×. At the same time, −1−1 and 52𝑘−352k−3 are two different elements orders of two, so −1 ∉⟨5⟩−1∉⟨5⟩. Therefore, ⟨ −1⟩⟨−1⟩ and ⟨5⟩⟨5⟩ have trivial intersection, so by the second isomorphism theorem

      (𝐙/2𝑘𝐙)×≅⟨−1⟩×⟨5⟩≅𝐶2×𝐶2𝑘−2.(Z/2kZ)×≅⟨−1⟩×⟨5⟩≅C2×C2k−2.
      • For the case where 𝑝p is an odd prime, it can be proven that (𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)×(Z/pkZ)× is isomorphic to the cyclic group 𝐶𝜑(𝑝𝑘)Cφ(pk).
      Proof

      To prove (𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)×(Z/pkZ)× is a cyclic group, using the fundamental theorem of finite abelian groups, we only need to prove that all its Sylow 𝑞q-subgroups are cyclic. First, for the Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup, direct calculation shows

      (1+𝑝)𝑝𝑘−1≡1(mod𝑝𝑘),(1+𝑝)𝑝𝑘−2≡1+𝑝𝑘−1(mod𝑝𝑘).(1+p)pk−1≡1(modpk),(1+p)pk−2≡1+pk−1(modpk).

      So, (1 +𝑝)(1+p) is an element of order 𝑝𝑘−1pk−1. That is, the unique Sylow 𝑝p-subgroup of (𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)×(Z/pkZ)× is the cyclic group ⟨1 +𝑝⟩⟨1+p⟩.

      For other Sylow 𝑞q-subgroups (𝑞 ≠𝑝q≠p), we can transform them to the case 𝑘 =1k=1 through group homomorphisms. Consider the group homomorphism 𝜑 :(𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)× →(𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×φ:(Z/pkZ)×→(Z/pZ)×, which maps the coset 𝑟 +𝑝𝑘𝐙r+pkZ to the coset 𝑟 +𝑝𝐙r+pZ. The size of this kernel is 𝑝𝑘−1pk−1, so when 𝜑φ is restricted to the Sylow 𝑞q-subgroup (𝑞 ≠𝑝q≠p) of (𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)×(Z/pkZ)×, the restricted homomorphism has trivial kernel, so this Sylow 𝑞q-subgroup is isomorphic to the image, i.e., the Sylow 𝑞q-subgroup of (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)×. Therefore, we only need to prove that the Sylow 𝑞q-subgroups of (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)× are all cyclic.

      Finally, prove that all Sylow 𝑞q-subgroups of (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)× are cyclic. Since (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)×(Z/pZ)× is a finite abelian group, we can decompose it by invariant factors as

      𝐶𝑛1×⋯×𝐶𝑛𝑟.Cn1×⋯×Cnr.

      Here, 𝑛1 ∣𝑛2 ∣⋯ ∣𝑛𝑟n1∣n2∣⋯∣nr. So each direct product factor has 𝑛1n1 elements whose orders divide 𝑛1n1. If 𝑟 >1r>1, then there are strictly more than 𝑛1n1 elements satisfying 𝑥𝑛1 =1xn1=1. But 𝐙/𝑝𝐙Z/pZ is a field, and polynomials of degree 𝑛1n1 over a field have at most 𝑛1n1 roots, so 𝑟 =1r=1. That is, (𝐙/𝑝𝐙)× ≅𝐶𝑝−1(Z/pZ)×≅Cp−1.

      This proves (𝐙/𝑝𝑘𝐙)× ≅𝐶𝑝𝑘−1 ×𝐶𝑝−1 =𝐶𝜑(𝑝𝑘)(Z/pkZ)×≅Cpk−1×Cp−1=Cφ(pk).

    The structure of the multiplicative group for general moduli is also determined. From existing results, the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n is a cyclic group if and only if the modulus 𝑛n is

    1,2,4,𝑝𝑘,2𝑝𝑘1,2,4,pk,2pk

    where 𝑝p is an odd prime; otherwise, the multiplicative group of integers modulo 𝑛n always has a subgroup 𝐶2 ×𝐶2C2×C2 and cannot be a cyclic group. When the multiplicative group is a cyclic group, the generator of the multiplicative group is called the primitive root of that modulus. Therefore, the theorem here gives exactly the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of primitive roots.

    Of course, the analysis of the multiplicative group structure contains more information than just the conditions for the existence of primitive roots. It clearly reflects the orders of different elements in the multiplicative group. Elements 𝑥x in the group (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)× satisfying 𝑥𝑘 =1xk=1, i.e., solutions to the congruence equation 𝑥𝑘 ≡1(mod𝑛)xk≡1(modn), are called 𝑘k-th roots of unity modulo 𝑛n; elements with order exactly equal to 𝑘k are called primitive 𝑘k-th roots of unity modulo 𝑛n. Using the structure of the multiplicative group, the existence and number of these roots can all be precisely calculated. Finally, the least common multiple of all orders of elements in (𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×(Z/nZ)×, i.e., the smallest positive integer 𝑘k such that 𝑥𝑘 =1xk=1 holds for all 𝑥 ∈(𝐙/𝑛𝐙)×x∈(Z/nZ)×, expressed as a function of 𝑛n, is the Carmichael function. Its series of properties can all be obtained from the structure of the multiplicative group.
